content:
Apple Vision Pro is one of the most interesting pieces of hardware Apple has ever made. Technically brilliant, but it's almost certainly a form factor that won't last — more like a transitional platform that introduces the world to visionOS, before we eventually get to real glasses.

I did actually buy one late last year, and while I don't use it a huge amount, there is one use case that makes it genuinely interesting.

When the Vision Pro launched, the potential seemed limitless. It was going to be the headset that killed all your screens. The Mac virtual display seemed compelling, so did the idea of spatial FaceTime — even if Persona was a bit jarring when it first appeared.

But once the honeymoon period passed, people realised the headset was heavy and difficult to wear for long periods. Plenty of people put their Vision Pros up for sale, which means you can pick one up second-hand at a substantial discount.

Second-hand prices are currently in the region of $1500, which is far more approachable than the $3699 starting price for a brand new one.

If the Vision Pro has a strength, it's watching content. The App Store in general isn't the most compelling, but most of the major streaming apps are there, including Disney+, HBO Max, and now even YouTube. Netflix is the biggest omission. Of course, you also have Apple TV.

The best way to enjoy Vision Pro

Outgoing Apple CEO Tim Cook shared his favourite Vision Pro use case back in January 2025, and mentioned it again last month in an interview for the premiere of Ted Lasso season 4:

I can't say I exclusively watch shows and movies on the Vision Pro. Sometimes it's just too much hassle, and the Vision Pro's software keyboard is poor, making multitasking occasionally painful.

But when I do watch shows and movies on the Vision Pro, I always use Tim Cook's method: lying down and looking up. It completely solves the weight problem, and if you have the time to invest, it's a remarkably relaxing experience.

At full price, the Vision Pro is an expensive product to use only occasionally as a TV. But given how much its value has dropped, I don't think buying one purely as a bedtime face-goggle TV is necessarily a bad idea. The experience is genuinely excellent, particularly in 3D.
